- NERC CIP-013 supply chain compliance challenges
- NERC CIP compliance monitoring enforcement program CMEP process
- NERC CIP INA ENA boundary transient electronic devices TEDs compliance challenges
- NERC CIP notice of penalty violation reports
- NERC CIP real-time operational needs cybersecurity conflicts
- FERC order NERC CIP compliance issues supply chain
- TSA pipeline cybersecurity directive NERC CIP comparison

---

**Fully Comprehensive Findings**

---

## 1. DESCRIPTION / OVERVIEW OF NERC CIP STANDARDS

### What Are the NERC CIP Standards?

NERC CIP (North American Electric Reliability Corporation Critical Infrastructure Protection) is a set of mandatory, FERC-enforceable cybersecurity and physical security standards that require registered entities to identify, categorize, and protect the cyber systems and physical assets of the Bulk Electric System (BES) in North America. [6][7][8][9][20]

NERC was formed in 1968 as a voluntary organization following the 1965 Northeast blackout that affected 30 million people. After the 2003 Northeast blackout (55 million people affected), the Energy Policy Act of 2005 authorized FERC to designate an Electric Reliability Organization (ERO), and NERC was selected. The first CIP standard was created, officially adopted in 2006, and approved by FERC in 2008. [8][9][20]

The NERC CIP framework is increasingly serving as a foundational model for emerging OT cybersecurity regulations globally. [8]

### Complete Set of Standards (CIP-002 through CIP-015)

As of 2026, 13-14 CIP standards are active (CIP-002 through CIP-015), with CIP-015 being the newest addition. [7][9][10][17][20]

**CIP-002 -- BES Cyber System Categorization** (CIP-002-5.1a, CIP-002-8 pending)
- Foundational scoping standard. Requires identification and categorization of BES Cyber Systems as High, Medium, or Low impact, determining which other standards apply. [6][7][8][9][10][19]
- Shifts from Version 4's "Critical Cyber Assets" approach to a "BES Cyber System" approach, aligning with the NIST Risk Management Framework. [19]
- BES Cyber Assets are defined by a real-time scoping characteristic: those that would adversely impact reliable operation within 15 minutes of compromise. Redundancy does not mitigate cyber security vulnerabilities. [19]
- Review/approval required at least once every 15 calendar months. [19]
- **CIP-002-8** (filed December 20, 2024, approved March 19, 2026) improves risk identification of Transmission Owner Control Centers by applying "bright-line" criteria and using weighted point values based on transmission voltages. Revises the Control Center definition to close ambiguity that allowed distributed control architectures, backup control centers, and cloud-hosted SCADA/EMS platforms to avoid high-impact CIP classification. [1][16][17]

**CIP-003 -- Security Management Controls** (CIP-003-8, CIP-003-9, CIP-003-11, CIP-003-12)
- Specifies consistent and sustainable security management controls establishing responsibility and accountability to protect BES Cyber Systems. [7][8][9][10][11]
- **CIP-003-9**: Enforcement began April 1, 2026, expanding governance requirements for low-impact BES Cyber Systems, focusing on vendor remote access and supply chain risk management. [7][17]
- **CIP-003-11**: Approved by FERC Order No. 918 on March 19, 2026. Adds controls to authenticate remote users, protect authentication information in transit, and detect malicious communications. Filed December 20, 2024. Effective date July 1, 2029. [1][11][16][17]
- **CIP-003-12**: NERC's draft proposes updates to align with new detection and incident reporting expectations, emphasizing monitoring inbound/outbound traffic for malicious communications and reinforcing baseline security for low-impact BES Cyber Systems. [1]
- Low-impact requirements include: Cyber Security Awareness (reinforced every 15 months), Physical Security Controls, Electronic Access Controls (inbound/outbound access controls, malicious communication detection, user authentication, authentication protection, vendor access determination/disablement, Dial-up Connectivity authentication), Cyber Security Incident Response (including E-ISAC notification, testing every 36 months, updates within 180 days), and TCA/Removable Media Malicious Code Risk Mitigation. [11]

**CIP-004 -- Personnel and Training** (CIP-004-6)
- Requires security awareness training at least every 15 months for personnel with access to BES Cyber Systems. Background checks required. [7][8][9][10][20]

**CIP-005 -- Electronic Security Perimeters** (CIP-005-6)
- Requires establishing ESPs as virtual zones isolating critical systems with controlled access points. Mandates authentication/encryption for remote access, monitoring of communications. [7][8][9][10][20]
- 2025 revisions strengthening controls around multi-factor authentication, session brokering, and termination of inactive sessions to mitigate third-party connection risks. [1]
- Being modified under Project 2025-06 (Supply Chain Risk Management) per FERC Order No. 912. [15]

**CIP-006 -- Physical Security of BES Cyber Systems** (CIP-006-6)
- Requires documented physical security plans, visitor control programs, and Physical Access Control System (PACS) testing every 2 years. [7][8][9][10][20]

**CIP-007 -- System Security Management** (CIP-007-6)
- Covers port/service management, security patching (must be evaluated at least once every 35 calendar days), malicious code prevention, and continuous security monitoring. [7][8][9][10][20]
- Particularly controversial due to prescriptive patch management requirements (every 35 days). [8]

**CIP-008 -- Incident Reporting and Response Planning** (CIP-008-6, CIP-008-7, CIP-008-8 proposed)
- Mandates documented incident response plans tested at least every 15 months. [7][8][9][10][12][20]
- **CIP-008-6** (effective January 1, 2021) expanded mandatory reporting to include incidents that compromise or attempt to compromise a utility's Electronic Security Perimeter (ESP) or Electronic Access Control or Monitoring Systems (EACMS), rather than only incidents that have caused actual disruption. [12][14]
- **CIP-008-7** was adopted by the NERC Board of Trustees on May 9, 2024. [13]
- **CIP-008-8** (Informal Draft 1, September 2025) is under development as part of Project 2022-05. Expands reporting to include: processes to identify, classify, and respond to Cyber Security Incidents; criteria to evaluate and define attempts to compromise; and notification requirements to E-ISAC and CISA. [13]

**CIP-009 -- Recovery Plans** (CIP-009-6)
- Focuses on business continuity with recovery plans tested every 15 months. Backup procedures required. [7][8][9][10][20]

**CIP-010 -- Configuration Change Management and Vulnerability Assessments** (CIP-010-3, CIP-010-6 proposed)
- Requires configuration monitoring every 35 days, vulnerability assessments every 15 months, and baseline configuration management. [7][8][9][10][20]
- **CIP-010-6** is under development in Project 2025-06 (Supply Chain Risk Management), with initial ballot conducted July 8-17, 2026 (Weighted Segment Value: 64.55). [15]

**CIP-011 -- Information Protection** (CIP-011-2)
- Safeguards sensitive BES Cyber System Information through classification, handling, storage, and disposal processes. [7][8][9][10][20]

**CIP-012 -- Communications Between Control Centers** (CIP-012-1, CIP-012-2)
- Mandates encryption for real-time monitoring data exchanged between control centers. [7][8][9][10][20]
- **CIP-012-2** effective July 1, 2026, strengthening protection of real-time operational data exchanged between control centers. [7][17]

**CIP-013 -- Supply Chain Risk Management** (CIP-013-1, CIP-013-3, CIP-013-4 proposed)
- Requires vendor risk management plans for medium/high-impact assets. Accelerated relevance after SolarWinds attack. [7][8][9][10][12][15][20]
- **CIP-013-4** (Draft 1, May 2026) responds to FERC Order No. 912. Requires: planning procurement to identify/assess cyber security risks (including spare equipment, emergency repairs, vendor transitions); procuring systems addressing vendor notification of incidents, coordinated incident responses, revocation of vendor access, disclosure of known vulnerabilities, verification of software integrity/authenticity; risk assessments prior to deployment (every 24 months for high impact, 36 months for medium impact); periodic post-deployment risk reassessment. Does not require renegotiating existing contracts. Board adoption anticipated October 7, 2026. [14][15]
- Supply chain cyber risks covered include: software vendors, hardware suppliers, cloud providers, managed service providers, contractors with system access, maintenance vendors, and remote support providers. [12]
- The NATF Supply Chain Security Criteria and Energy Sector Supply Chain Risk Questionnaire (Version 7.0, May 26, 2026) provides industry tools for CIP-013 compliance, with updates for NIST SP 800-171r3 and NIST SP 800-53r5.2.0 mappings. [13]

**CIP-014 -- Physical Security** (CIP-014-3)
- Originated from FERC Order No. 802 (November 2014) following the April 2013 Metcalf substation attack in California (attackers fired more than 100 rounds into 17 electrical transformers, causing $15 million in damage). [6][7][8][10]
- Requires risk assessments (every 30-60 months), third-party verification, threat/vulnerability assessments, documented physical security plans (deter, detect, delay, assess, respond), and third-party reviews. [7][10]
- Applicability primarily determined by transmission voltage: 500kV+ generally applicable; 200-499kV when connected to 3+ substations at 200kV+. [7]

**CIP-015 -- Internal Network Security Monitoring (INSM)** (CIP-015-1, CIP-015-2)
- **CIP-015-1**: Established May 9, 2024, in response to FERC Order No. 887. Mandates monitoring network traffic within Electronic Security Perimeters (ESPs) to detect malicious activity via risk-justified data feeds or sensors placed within the ESP. Addresses "east-west" traffic visibility gaps that perimeter defenses miss. [1][7][17][20]
- Effective September 2, 2025. [1][7]
- Phased compliance: September 2, 2028 for high-impact and control center medium-impact systems; September 2, 2030 for other medium-impact systems. [7][17]
- **CIP-015-2**: Approved by FERC on August 10, 2026 (RD26-6-000). Expands INSM requirements. [17]

### Major Revisions and New Standards Approved by FERC in 2024-2026

**FERC Order No. 907 (June 26, 2025)** -- Approved CIP-015-1 (Internal Network Security Monitoring). [1][7]

## 2. REPORTING TIMELINES

### Incident Reporting Requirements under NERC CIP

Under **CIP-008-6** (effective January 1, 2021), mandatory reporting was expanded to include incidents that **compromise or attempt to compromise** a utility's Electronic Security Perimeter (ESP) or Electronic Access Control or Monitoring Systems (EACMS), rather than only incidents that have caused actual disruption. [12]

**CIP-008-8** (Informal Draft 1, September 2025) further expands reporting requirements. [13]

### Timeline for Reporting to E-ISAC and CISA

Under **CIP-008-8** (proposed), entities must notify the Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center (E-ISAC) and, if subject to U.S. jurisdiction, the Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) of Events of Interest that meet the definition of either an Attempted Cyber Security Incident or a Cyber Security Incident. [13]

**Reporting timelines under CIP-008-8:**
- **1 hour** after determination of a **Reportable Cyber Security Incident** [13]
- **By end of next calendar day** after determination of an **Attempted Cyber Security Incident** [13]
- **Updates** must be provided within **7 calendar days** of new or changed attribute information [13]

**Required initial notification attributes:**
- Functional impact
- Attack vector used
- Actionable intelligence (including level of intrusion achieved/attempted) [13]

### 2023 Incident Reporting Statistics

In 2023, only three CIP-008-6 reports were submitted to the E-ISAC (down from eight in 2022), distributed across NPCC, SERC, and WECC regions. All three involved unique attack vectors with no common tactics, techniques, or procedures: [14]

1. **Ransomware attack** on a third-party supporting a plant maintenance management system (system inoperable for hours, site data compromised)
2. **Malware infection** from a contractor accessing the internet via an emissions control system, which infected IT systems (quickly isolated, no reliability impact)
3. **Physical and cyber intrusion** by a vendor who accessed the ID badging system and granted unauthorized access to 19 vendor employees to high-impact BES Cyber Systems and ERC Zones

None of the three 2023 incidents were classified as "Reportable Cyber Security Incidents" (they were considered attempts to compromise). Over three years (2021-2023), the E-ISAC received a total of 13 reports, none of which were Reportable Cyber Security Incidents. Malware accounted for approximately 50% of all reported incidents across the three-year period. All three 2023 incidents involved contracted employees. [14]

### The E-ISAC

The Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center (E-ISAC) serves as a trusted security hub for North America's electricity industry, helping members strengthen defenses against evolving cyber and physical security threats. Functions include: gathering, analyzing, and sharing information about threats and mitigations; sharing timely alerts and analysis; providing secure communication channels for members; and facilitating information sharing across industry and government. It works closely with the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Electricity Subsector Coordinating Council (ESCC). Operated by NERC, the E-ISAC is organizationally isolated from NERC's enforcement processes. Membership is open to North American electricity and natural gas industry asset owners/operators, plus qualifying government and cross-sector partners. The 2025 E-ISAC End-of-Year Report noted that 2025 marked an unprecedented year of new and evolving threats, with the E-ISAC serving over 1,900 member and partner organizations. [15]

### Self-Reporting Obligations for Compliance Violations

The ERO Enterprise values high levels of self-reported noncompliance as an indicator of strong detective controls and compliance culture. [16] Enforcement Cause Codes were added to the Align tool for registered entities in September 2025, with nearly 60% of submitted findings including them. [17]

NERC's Enforcement program assesses risk and root causes of noncompliance, ensures mitigation of violations, and uses a risk-based approach to determine disposition methods. Entities found in violation must submit and complete mitigation. [19]

### Difference Between "Reporting" and "Compliance" Timelines

"Reporting" timelines refer to the notifications required under CIP-008 when a Cyber Security Incident occurs (1 hour for reportable incidents, by end of next calendar day for attempted incidents). "Compliance" timelines refer to recurring obligations under various CIP standards, such as:
- CIP-002 categorization review: every 15 calendar months [19]
- CIP-004 training: at least every 15 months [20]
- CIP-007 patch evaluation: at least every 35 calendar days [10][20]
- CIP-008 incident response plan testing: every 15 months [20]
- CIP-009 recovery plan testing: every 15 months [10][20]
- CIP-010 vulnerability assessments: every 15 months [10][20]
- CIP-013 plan review and approval: every 15 months [12][14]
- CIP-014 risk assessments: every 30-60 months [10]

## 3. COVERED-ENTITY DEFINITIONS

### Which Entities Are Covered? (Registered Entities under NERC's Compliance Registry)

The standards apply to "Registered Entities" under NERC's compliance registry, including: [10][11][19]
- Balancing Authorities
- Distribution Providers (with specific BES protection facilities, including UFLS/UVLS systems of 300 MW+, Special Protection Systems/Remedial Action Schemes, Protection Systems, Cranking Paths/Blackstart Resources)
- Generator Operators
- Generator Owners
- Interchange Coordinators/Authorities
- Reliability Coordinators
- Transmission Operators
- Transmission Owners
- RTOs and ISOs

All bulk power system owners, operators, and users must comply with NERC-approved Reliability Standards and are required to register with NERC through the appropriate Regional Entity. [18]

### What is the "Bulk Electric System" (BES) Definition?

The BES (also known as the Bulk Power System or BPS) encompasses the electrical generation resources, transmission lines, interconnections, and associated equipment operated at 100 kV or higher. [18] Real-time and non-real-time BES Cyber Assets are defined as those Cyber Assets that, if rendered unavailable, degraded, or misused, would adversely impact the reliable operation of the BES within 15 minutes of the activation or exercise of the compromise. [19]

### Bright-Line Criteria and Inclusion/Exclusion Processes

The impact rating criteria in **CIP-002 (Attachment 1)** establish bright-line thresholds for categorization: [19]

**High Impact (H):**
- Control Centers/backup Control Centers used by: Reliability Coordinator; Balancing Authority (≥3000 MW aggregate generation in single Interconnection); Transmission Operator and Generator Operator (for assets meeting specific criteria)

**Medium Impact (M):** BES Cyber Systems not in High Impact, associated with:
1. Generation ≥1500 MW at single plant location
2. Reactive resources ≥1000 MVAR at single location
3. Generation Facilities designated by Planning Coordinator/Transmission Planner as necessary to avoid Adverse Reliability Impact (>1 year horizon)
4. Transmission Facilities at 500 kV or higher
5. Transmission Facilities between 200-499 kV at stations with aggregate weighted value >3000 (weighted by voltage)
6. Facilities critical to IROL derivation
7. Facilities essential to Nuclear Plant Interface Requirements
8. Transmission Facilities for generation interconnection where loss would affect generation ≥1500 MW
9. SPS/RAS/automated switching that would cause IROL violations
10. Automatic load shedding (UFLS/UVLS) ≥300 MW
11. Control Centers for Generator Operator ≥1500 MW or Transmission Operator (not already High Impact)
12. Control Centers monitoring/controlling BES Transmission Lines with aggregate weighted value >6000
13. Control Centers for Balancing Authority ≥1500 MW

**CIP-002-8** improves risk identification of Transmission Owner Control Centers by applying "bright-line" criteria using weighted point values based on transmission voltages. [1][16]

### Low, Medium, and High Impact BES Asset Categories

**High Impact:** Control Centers used by Reliability Coordinators, large Balancing Authorities, and Transmission Operators/Generator Operators meeting specific criteria. Subject to the most stringent requirements across all CIP standards. [19]

**Medium Impact:** BES Cyber Systems meeting any of the 13 medium-impact criteria (including generation ≥1500 MW, transmission ≥500 kV, critical IROL facilities, etc.). [19]

**Low Impact:** All BES Cyber Systems for Facilities not included in High or Medium Impact criteria default to Low Impact. Associated with Control Centers, Transmission stations/substations, generation resources, restoration systems, SPS/RAS, and qualifying Distribution Provider systems. [19]

**Critical distinction:** Low-impact BES Cyber Systems still carry real obligations under CIP-003, including cybersecurity plans, vendor remote access controls, and transient device policies. Entities that treat low impact as "exempt" are consistently surprised by audit findings. [6]

### Exemptions

Exemptions from CIP standards include: Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission-regulated facilities, communication networks/data links between Electronic Security Perimeters, NRC-regulated cyber systems under 10 C.F.R. Section 73.54, and non-qualifying Distribution Provider systems. [11][13][19]

## 4. ENFORCEMENT MECHANISMS

### How NERC Enforces CIP Standards

NERC is the Electric Reliability Organization (ERO) under FERC oversight. The **Compliance Monitoring and Enforcement Program (CMEP)** is the primary mechanism for assessing, investigating, measuring, and evaluating compliance with NERC's Reliability Standards. [18][19]

Enforcement assesses risk and root causes of reported noncompliance, analyzes trends, and can issue directives to address violations. Sanctions are determined pursuant to the factors laid out in the NERC Sanction Guidelines. Entities found in violation must submit and complete mitigation. NERC maintains an appeals process and provides a Consistency Reporting Tool for reporting perceived inconsistencies across Regional Entities. [19]

### Role of FERC in Enforcement

FERC oversees NERC as the ERO, certifies NERC's delegation agreements with Regional Entities, approves reliability standards, and can impose penalties. FERC's Office of Enforcement investigates violations and approves Stipulation and Consent Agreements. [1][2][4]

FERC continues to play an active role in working with NERC and regional entities to ensure BPS reliability, accelerated by interconnection of diverse generation resources, extreme demand from data centers, and Administration directives. [4]

### Compliance Monitoring and Enforcement Program (CMEP)

The CMEP is the ERO Enterprise's framework for compliance monitoring and enforcement. Key elements include: [17][18][19]

- **Audits** on 3-6 year cycles [7]
- **Self-reports** and periodic data submittals [7]
- **Find, Fix, Track and Report (FFT)** program for minor violations
- **Compliance Exception (CE)** program for minimal risk noncompliance
- **Potential Noncompliance (PNC)** abeyance period as a mechanism to strengthen feedback to Standards development [17]
- **Reliability Standard Audit Worksheets (RSAWs)** for documenting compliance evidence [17]
- **Self-Logging Program** for registered entities [9]

**2025 CMEP Developments:**
- The 2026 CMEP Implementation Plan shifts focus from compliance evaluation to proactive risk mitigation. [17]
- Six Align tool releases (7.1.0 through 7.5.0) with various module improvements. [17]
- Enforcement Cause Codes added to Align in September 2025, with nearly 60% of submitted findings including them. [17]
- The ERO Enterprise aims to process minimal risk Compliance Exceptions within 180 days on average. [17]
- The ERO's violation backlog dropped by nearly 50% in 2025. [10][6]

### Investigative Processes for Violations

NERC's Enforcement program investigates all noncompliance identified by Compliance Enforcement Authorities (CEAs - typically Regional Entities) under the CMEP. The process includes: [19]

1. Identification of noncompliance (through audits, self-reports, or investigations)
2. Preliminary screening
3. Risk assessment and root cause analysis
4. Determination of disposition method (FFT, CE, Notice of Penalty, etc.)
5. Mitigation plan development and submission
6. Mitigation completion and verification
7. Appeals process available

The 2024 annual review found Regional Entities processing violations appropriately, with all sampled noncompliance adequately remediated and root causes clearly identified. [16]

## 5. PENALTY STRUCTURES

### Penalty Structures for NERC CIP Violations

Violations are classified by **Violation Risk Factor (VRF)** and **Violation Severity Level (VSL)**, with penalties determined by the NERC Sanction Guidelines. [7][19]

**Violation Risk Factors (VRF):** [11][19]
- **High** - Could directly cause or contribute to Bulk Electric System instability, separation, or cascading failures
- **Medium** - Could directly cause or contribute to BES instability, but with lower severity
- **Lower** - Administrative or procedural noncompliance

**Violation Severity Levels (VSL):** [11][13]
- Lower
- Moderate
- High
- Severe

### Maximum Civil Penalty Per Violation Per Day

- When the program was first introduced, penalties were capped at $1 million per day per violation. [6][7][8][9][10][20]
- By 2025, this maximum penalty had risen to **$1.54 million per day per violation** (FERC-adjusted for inflation). [6]
- As of 2026, the maximum penalty is **$1.25 million per day** per some sources, or **$1.54 million** per others depending on the year of adjustment. [9]
- A **Penalty Inflation Adjustment Notice** was issued on July 2, 2026. [9]
- Aggregate fines can exceed $10 million for systemic violations. [7]

### How Penalty Severity Levels Are Determined

Penalties are determined based on: [19]
- Violation Risk Factor (the potential impact of the noncompliance)
- Violation Severity Level (the extent of the noncompliance)
- Duration of the violation
- History of prior violations
- Good faith efforts to comply
- Self-reporting and cooperation
- Root cause analysis

### Specific Penalties Imposed in 2024-2026

**2023:** NERC issued $10.5 million in penalties for CIP violations across 22 separate enforcement actions. [8]

**Notable historical penalties:**
- Duke Energy: $10 million penalty for 127 violations across CIP standards (2019) [7]
- Unidentified entity: $2.7 million penalty (2018) [7]
- PG&E: $2.7 million penalty (2017) [7]

**NERC redacts the identity of most violating entities** on public CIP Notices of Penalty, because publishing specific security weaknesses of a named bulk-electric-system facility could itself create risk. [5]

## 6. REAL-WORLD COMPLIANCE CHALLENGES (2024-2026)

### Specific NERC Violation Reports or Notices of Penalty

- **2025 NERC Enforcement Actions:** Entergy Corporation (September 2025), Grande Prairie Wind, LLC (July 2025), Hamilton Liberty/Essential Power Rock Springs (March 2025), American Electric Power Service Corporation (January 2025) [8]
- **2024 Enforcement Trends:** 20% increase in penalties over the previous year [1]

### Challenges with Supply Chain Cybersecurity (CIP-013 Compliance)

FERC Order No. 912 (September 18, 2025) directed NERC to submit new/modified reliability standards within 18 months addressing gaps in CIP standards related to supply chain risk management. [4][14][15]

Common CIP-013 compliance challenges include: [12]
- Siloed procurement and cybersecurity processes
- Inconsistent vendor risk assessments
- Weak contract language
- Limited visibility into vendor access
- Poor tracking of vendor incidents
- Manual evidence collection
- Difficulty proving implementation during audits

The greatest risks often come from trusted relationships -- a vendor with access to critical systems, sensitive data, or OT environments can create significant exposure if its own controls are weak. [12]

**Project 2025-06 (Supply Chain Risk Management)** responds to FERC Order No. 912 by modifying CIP-005, CIP-010, and CIP-013 to address gaps in identifying, assessing, and responding to supply chain risks, and to extend SCRM applicability to Protected Cyber Assets (PCAs). The initial ballot for CIP-010-6 (Weighted Segment Value: 64.55) and CIP-013-4 (Weighted Segment Value: 30.64) was conducted July 8-17, 2026. [15]

### Challenges with Transitioning to New Standards Versions

The compliance environment for energy and critical infrastructure organizations changed significantly in early 2026. FERC approved five new reliability standards for inverter-based resources, updated the NERC CIP control center definition, finalized rules on virtualization, and introduced mandatory cybersecurity controls for low-impact BES Cyber Systems, all within weeks of one another. [1]

**CIP-003-9** enforcement began April 1, 2026, expanding governance requirements for low-impact BES Cyber Systems. Vendor remote access at smaller substations and remote facilities is identified as the most likely area of non-compliance. [1][7]

**CIP-015-1** became effective September 2, 2025, with phased compliance deadlines through September 2030. [7]

**CIP-012-2** took effect July 1, 2026. [7][17]

**Virtualization Standards (Order No. 919):** Entities must comply with 11 updated CIP standards (CIP-002-7 through CIP-013-3) by July 1, 2028. [2][17]

A NERC white paper (December 2024) identified major barriers to adopting new technologies while maintaining CIP compliance, including: workforce shortages, financing limitations, rigid compliance approaches, and a standards development process that lags behind technology innovation. [2]

### Internal Network (INA) and External Network (ENA) Boundary Challenges

The CIP framework requires clear delineation between Internal Networks (INAs) and External Networks (ENAs) through Electronic Security Perimeters (ESPs). Key challenges include: [6][20]

- Maintaining accurate real-time asset inventories [20]
- Visibility gaps between IT and OT environments [20]
- Centralized access control across remote locations [20]
- Treating low-impact as "low-effort" (entities that treat low impact as exempt are consistently surprised by audit findings) [6]

**CIP-015-1** (Internal Network Security Monitoring) was specifically adopted to address the lack of internal visibility in existing CIP standards. Firewalls protect network edges, while CIP-015-1 ensures visibility and helps detect lateral movement and internal threats that traditional perimeter defenses may overlook. [20]

### Transient Electronic Devices (TEDs) Compliance Challenges

Under CIP-003-11 (R2), low-impact BES Cyber Systems require documented cyber security plans covering "TCA/Removable Media Malicious Code Risk Mitigation" (Transient Cyber Assets and Removable Media). [11] The management of Transient Electronic Devices (laptops, USB drives, test equipment, contractor devices) that connect to BES Cyber Systems remains a significant compliance challenge, particularly for remote substations and field operations.

### Conflicts Between Real-Time Operational Needs and Cybersecurity Controls

OT systems have unique constraints that create inherent tensions with cybersecurity controls: [7][8]
- 15-30+ year lifecycles for equipment
- Limited patching windows (can't take critical systems offline during operation)
- Proprietary protocols (Modbus, DNP3, IEC 61850) that complicate security monitoring
- Operational consequences from security tool deployment (e.g., vulnerability scanning can disrupt operations)
- Patches must be evaluated at least once every 35 calendar days under CIP-007, but applying patches in OT environments can be operationally risky [10]

**CIP-010 vulnerability assessments** take 4-8 weeks per site, require 80+ hours of staff time, and cost $50K-$100K+ with consultants. 95% of entities default to "paper" assessments that rarely reflect the true state of OT environments. [9]

### Cybersecurity Threat Landscape

- IBM's 2025 X-Force Threat Intelligence Index reports that 70% of all cyberattacks they responded to involve critical infrastructure targets, with over 25% exploiting vulnerabilities in outdated systems. [20]
- The energy sector accounted for 10% of all incidents in 2024. [20]
- The FBI IC3 reported a 9% rise in ransomware complaints targeting U.S. critical infrastructure in 2024. [20]
- Global critical infrastructure suffered 420 million attacks across 163 countries in 2023 (30% YoY increase), equivalent to 13 attacks per second, with one-third of attacks targeting protocols used in automation and power. [11]
- Gartner predicts 30% of critical infrastructure organizations will face a severe cyberattack by 2025. [20]
- The 2019 sPower incident was the first cyberattack with operational power grid impact in the U.S., targeting an exposed Cisco firewall with a known vulnerability used by an independent power producer. [12]
- The 2022 Viasat KA-SAT network attack affected 5,800 wind turbines in Europe. [12]
- The Ukraine Industroyer attacks (2016, 2022) and FrostyGoop (2024) exploited unencrypted protocols (Modbus, IEC 104, IEC 61850). [12]

### Idaho National Laboratory Report on Gaps Beyond NERC CIP Perimeters

A December 2025 Idaho National Laboratory report (INL/RPT-25-89588) identified a critical cybersecurity gap: while NERC CIP standards secure equipment within facility perimeters, all communications infrastructure beyond Electronic Access Points (EAPs) remains largely unregulated. This includes: [12]

- Control center-to-substation/generation plant communications
- Dispatchable distribution-level generation signals
- Inter-substation SCADA traffic
- Distribution automation signals
- Third-party telecom provider networks

The report provides six recommendations: (1) Enforce strong boundary control, (2) Ensure all devices are part of patch management plans, (3) Use secure protocols where available, (4) Implement strong procurement language (SBOMs, secure update processes), (5) Enforce strong access control (MFA, RBAC, time-bound access), and (6) Strengthen logging and monitoring for communications assets. [12]

### Common Compliance Audit Failures

The five most common audit failures identified across industry sources: [8][10]
1. CIP-002 categorization gaps (failing to re-review categorization after facility changes)
2. CIP-005 ESP boundary violations
3. CIP-007 patch management issues (manual processes can't keep up)
4. CIP-004 access management failures (failing to revoke access within 24 hours of role changes/termination)
5. CIP-010 configuration baseline problems (treating change management as IT process rather than formal compliance control)

**Root Cause Analysis:** Across all reliability standards, non-compliance is rarely the result of one missed form -- it's a symptom of deeper, systematic process challenges. The biggest compliance failures are usually: handoffs that didn't happen, reminders that didn't fire, SMEs who left and took the process with them, and inconsistent documentation. [10][11]

# SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Rules in 2026

#### Table of Contents

* Introduction
* SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Requirements: Quick Comparison
* What Counts as a Cybersecurity Incident?
* SEC Cybersecurity Compliance Workflow
* Common SEC Cyber Disclosure Gaps
* How Compliance Software Helps With SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Readiness
* Frequently Asked Questions

The [SEC’s cybersecurity disclosure](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/2023/07/s7-09-22) rules changed the expectations for public companies by requiring faster, more structured disclosure of material cybersecurity incidents along with greater transparency into how organizations govern and manage cyber risk.For many organizations, the challenge is not simply understanding the rule itself. The challenge is operationalizing it. Security teams, legal departments, compliance officers, investor relations, executives, and boards must now work together under tight timelines to assess incidents, determine materiality, document decisions, manage evidence, and support defensible disclosures. A delayed escalation, fragmented evidence trail, or unclear ownership can quickly become a disclosure risk.This is why SEC cybersecurity disclosure compliance has become more than a reporting obligation. It has become a test of organizational readiness, governance maturity, and operational coordination. Companies are now expected to demonstrate not only that they can respond to cyber incidents, but also that they can prove how risks are identified, escalated, reviewed, disclosed, and governed across the organization.

This guide explains the SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules in 2026, including Form 8-K Item 1.05 requirements, annual cybersecurity governance disclosures, materiality assessments, reporting timelines, compliance workflows, common mistakes, and how organizations can strengthen disclosure readiness through structured compliance and risk management processes.

## What Are the SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Rules?

The SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules require public companies to provide more consistent and timely disclosures about material cybersecurity incidents and their cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance processes.

The SEC adopted the final rules to improve the consistency and comparability of cyber-related disclosures for investors. The rules created a specific current disclosure requirement for material cybersecurity incidents and centralized annual disclosures around cybersecurity governance and risk management.

In simple terms, companies must be able to answer:

* Was there a cybersecurity incident?
* Was it material?
* When was materiality determined?
* What was the nature, scope, and timing of the incident?
* What is the material impact or reasonably likely material impact?
* How does the company identify and manage cybersecurity risks?
* What role does management play?
* What role does the board play?

![Understanding Cybersecurity Risk Management](https://www.v-comply.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Understanding-Cybersecurity-Risk-Management.png)

## SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Requirements: Quick Comparison

| Requirement | Where It Is Disclosed | What Companies Must Do | Why It Matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Material cybersecurity incident disclosure | Form 8-K Item 1.05 | Disclose within four business days after materiality determination | Gives investors timely information |
| Cybersecurity risk management | Annual report | Describe processes for identifying and managing cyber risks | Shows operational maturity |
| Cybersecurity strategy | Annual report | Explain how cyber risks affect business strategy, operations, or financial condition | Connects cyber risk to enterprise risk |
| Cybersecurity governance | Annual report | Describe board oversight and management’s role | Shows accountability |
| Updates to incomplete incident information | Amended Form 8-K | Update missing or unavailable information later | Prevents incomplete disclosure gaps |

## Who Must Comply?

The SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules apply to public companies that are subject to Exchange Act reporting requirements. This includes many U.S. public companies and foreign private issuers with relevant SEC reporting obligations.

The rules matter most for:

* Public company legal teams
* Compliance officers
* CISOs and security leaders
* Risk management teams
* Internal audit teams
* Investor relations teams
* Board and audit committee members
* Disclosure committees
* Incident response teams

## What Counts as a Cybersecurity Incident?

A cybersecurity incident can include unauthorized access, data theft, ransomware, system compromise, credential abuse, business email compromise, data exposure, cloud misconfiguration, vendor-related breach, or disruption affecting critical systems.

The key question under the SEC rule is not simply whether an incident occurred. The key question is whether the incident is **material** to investors.

That means companies need a documented process to assess materiality across legal, financial, operational, reputational, regulatory, and business impact factors.

## The Four-Business-Day Disclosure Rule

A material cybersecurity incident must be disclosed on Form 8-K Item 1.05 within four business days after the company determines that the incident is material. The clock starts at materiality determination, not necessarily the moment the incident is discovered.

This makes documentation critical. Companies need to track:

* Date and time of incident detection
* Date and time of escalation
* Who reviewed the incident
* What evidence was considered
* When materiality was assessed
* When materiality was determined
* Who approved the disclosure
* What information was unavailable at the time
* Follow-up amendments, if required

## What Must Be Included in an Item 1.05 Form 8-K?

For a material cybersecurity incident, companies must disclose the material aspects of the incident’s:

* Nature
* Scope
* Timing
* Material impact
* Reasonably likely material impact

The SEC has also clarified that if a company has not yet determined the impact or reasonably likely impact, it should still disclose the material incident and update the filing later when that information becomes available.

## Annual Cybersecurity Governance Disclosure

The SEC rules also require annual disclosure about cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance. These disclosures are intended to help investors understand how a company manages cybersecurity threats as business risks.

Companies should be prepared to explain:

* Processes for identifying cybersecurity risks
* Processes for assessing cybersecurity risks
* Processes for managing cybersecurity risks
* Whether third-party risks are included
* How cyber risks affect business strategy
* Board oversight of cybersecurity risks
* Management’s role and cybersecurity expertise
* Escalation and reporting structures

## SEC Cybersecurity Compliance Workflow

| Step | Action | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Detect cybersecurity event | Security / IT |
| 2 | Escalate to incident response team | CISO / Security Lead |
| 3 | Document facts and affected systems | Security / Legal |
| 4 | Assess business, legal, financial, and operational impact | Legal / Finance / Risk |
| 5 | Determine materiality | Disclosure Committee / Legal / Executives |
| 6 | Prepare Form 8-K Item 1.05 if material | Legal / Investor Relations |
| 7 | Track unresolved details | Compliance / Legal |
| 8 | File amendment if needed | Legal / SEC Reporting |
| 9 | Update controls and corrective actions | Compliance / Risk / Security |
| 10 | Report lessons learned to leadership and board | CISO / Compliance / Board Committee |

## Why This Matters in 2026

SEC cybersecurity disclosure compliance is not only a legal disclosure issue. It is an operational governance issue.

Companies need a reliable way to connect:

* Incident response
* Cybersecurity risk management
* Legal review
* Materiality assessment
* Board reporting
* Control testing
* Vendor risk
* Evidence collection
* Corrective action tracking
* Disclosure approvals

Without a structured workflow, teams may struggle to prove how decisions were made, when they were made, and who was accountable.

## Common SEC Cyber Disclosure Gaps

| Gap | Why It Creates Risk |
| --- | --- |
| No documented materiality workflow | Hard to prove disclosure timing |
| Scattered incident records | Incomplete evidence trail |
| Weak board reporting | Governance disclosure risk |
| No defined cyber risk ownership | Accountability gaps |
| Manual escalation | Delayed legal review |
| Vendor incidents not integrated | Third-party exposure |
| No corrective action tracking | Repeat findings |
| Generic annual disclosures | Boilerplate risk |

## How Compliance Software Helps With SEC Cybersecurity Disclosure Readiness

A compliance management platform like VComply can help organizations manage the operating layer behind SEC cyber disclosure readiness.

Key capabilities include:

* Assigning ownership for cybersecurity controls
* Tracking incident response workflows
* Documenting escalation timelines
* Maintaining evidence for materiality review
* Linking risks to controls and corrective actions
* Tracking policy reviews and employee acknowledgments
* Managing third-party risk tasks
* Creating audit-ready reports
* Giving leadership visibility into open cyber compliance gaps

The goal is not to automate legal judgment. The goal is to make sure the organization has the evidence, ownership, workflows, and documentation needed to support timely and defensible decisions.

## Frequently Asked Questions

Here are some of the most frequently asked questions about SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules.

### What are the SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules?

The SEC cybersecurity disclosure rules require public companies to disclose material cybersecurity incidents and provide annual disclosures about cybersecurity risk management, strategy, and governance.

### When must a cybersecurity incident be disclosed to the SEC?

A material cybersecurity incident must be disclosed on Form 8-K Item 1.05 within four business days after the company determines that the incident is material.

### Does the four-day deadline start when the incident is discovered?

No. The deadline starts after the company determines that the cybersecurity incident is material, not necessarily when the incident is first discovered.

### What must companies disclose in Form 8-K Item 1.05?

Companies must disclose the material aspects of the nature, scope, and timing of the incident, as well as its material impact or reasonably likely material impact.

### What annual cybersecurity disclosures are required?

Companies must disclose information about cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, board oversight, and management’s role in managing material cybersecurity risks.

### How can compliance software help with SEC cybersecurity disclosure readiness?

Compliance software helps organizations document incident workflows, assign owners, track evidence, manage risks, monitor corrective actions, and maintain audit trails that support timely and defensible disclosure decisions.

This webpage tracks the U.S. Chamber of Commerce's legal challenge to the SEC's Climate Disclosure Rule, filed in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit (Docket 24-1522). The case timeline includes:

- **March 14, 2024**: U.S. Chamber, Texas Association of Business, and Longview Chamber of Commerce filed a petition for review challenging the SEC's final climate disclosure rule, arguing it erodes the reasonable investor standard of materiality.
- **March 26, 2024**: Motion for stay pending review filed.
- **April 4, 2024**: SEC entered a discretionary stay of its climate disclosure rule pending judicial review.
- **March 27, 2025**: SEC dropped its defense of the Climate Disclosure Rule.
- **April 24, 2025**: Eighth Circuit placed the case in abeyance following SEC's announcement. The rule remains stayed and has never gone into effect.
- **September 12, 2025**: Case placed into indefinite abeyance; SEC expressed it does not intend to enforce the rule.
- **May 8, 2026**: Chamber and co-petitioners moved for vacatur of the rule after SEC announced it would undertake notice-and-comment rulemaking to rescind the rule.
- **May 21, 2026**: Eighth Circuit denied the motion to vacate the SEC's climate disclosure rule.

The case is currently pending. Eugene Scalia and attorneys from Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher LLP served as outside counsel.

# Navigating Privacy and Cybersecurity Laws in 2026 Will Prove Difficult

No matter what new laws or regulations make the cut for 2026, it's clear that compliance challenges will persist and federal legislation will be limited.

![Picture of Arielle Waldman](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blte685016783fc7faa/67ca10f9cf523d2a3ce48c04/arielle_waldman_headshot.jpg?width=100&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale "Picture of Arielle Waldman")

January 12, 2026

![](https://eu-images.contentstack.com/v3/assets/blt6d90778a997de1cd/blt4602d9695ec3e1f1/69655ab9ae1d94027b8f024c/HWP2C7.jpg?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=80&disable=upscale)

Keeping up with new privacy and cybersecurity laws has proved challenging for enterprises, many of which struggle to understand which laws even apply to them. Artificial intelligence (AI) complicates matters further, expanding [data and privacy concerns](https://www.techtarget.com/searchsecurity/tip/State-of-data-privacy-laws) with increased third-party risks. New tools also introduce data collection and sharing challenges, regulation complexities, and different attack vectors.

That trend will continue into 2026.

Updated laws and legislation try to reflect that to protect valuable data and individual privacy. In 2025, the Department of Justice (DoJ) announced compliance for a new Data Security Program, the Federal Trade Commission updated the [Children's Online Privacy Protection Act](/data-privacy/new-coppa-rules-children-data-privacy-concerns), and the US Department of Health and Human Services proposed amendments to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act security rule.

All three highlight how drastically the landscape has evolved over the past 10 years, demonstrating how tricky compliance is for organizations. While it's difficult to predict what new privacy and cybersecurity laws will emerge in 2026 — especially on the federal level — it's clear that compliance struggles will remain.

Related:[CISOs Break Their Silence in 'Declassified' Docuseries](/cyber-risk/cisos-break-their-silence-in-declassified-docuseries)

"It's made more challenging by the frequency of how quickly things change in the environment," says David Saunders, privacy and cybersecurity partner at McDermott, Will, and Schulte. "I get it, but it's hard to expect compliance from companies when it's constantly changing. At some point, it has a deterrent effect on compliance."

## What's on the Docket for 2026?

Compliance will likely mean a big project for enterprises to undertake in 2026. Many companies are still striving to adhere to laws announced or passed in 2025. However, many lessons can be applied when the new laws are eventually settled.

Three main legal actions — minimum age requirements for apps, expanded data privacy requirements, and regulations on AI use in human resources — are priorities for US clients of McDermott, Will and Schulte, Saunders says.

App age signal laws continue to be a top concern. US state regulations would require app stores, such as Google and Apple, and developers to verify ages during downloads and — at least in theory — for purchases.

In late December, a federal judge temporarily blocked a Texas Senate bill, otherwise known as the App Store Accountability Act, that was slated to go into effect on Jan. 1. A similar law in Louisiana was struck down by the state supreme court in December (the state attorney general said she will appeal), but another in Utah was enacted in mid-2025.

Related:[Sherlock Holmes Was the 'OG' Social Engineer](/cyber-risk/sherlock-holmes-was-the-og-social-engineer)

Companies are focused on the issue regardless because Apple and Google have put out their API documentation, Saunders says. Some developers may have scrambled to change code to comply with new frameworks and standards under strict deadlines. The API documentation also put additional responsibility on developers to ensure they're gating content restricted for children under 13, for example.

Many companies are reeling to understand the Texas law and are on alert for what will happen in Utah and Louisiana.

"It's still front-of-mind because the laws were first of their kind," Saunders says.

Many companies were left scrambling to prepare at year-end, only to have the courts enjoin the laws days before they were to take effect, he said. Additionally, the appeals leave matters in the air, he says.

"I anticipate legal challenges, but, in the meantime, companies at least have to prepare," Saunders adds.

Makeup companies and enterprises that derive money from advertising, in particular, are struggling with what to do with age limit laws, he says. Every SKU for sale in the app must have an age assigned to it, and for some companies that could mean a wide range of items. Implementation challenges stem from a lack of time.

Related:[More Countries Jump on the Social Media 'Ban Wagon'](/cyber-risk/more-countries-jump-on-the-social-media-ban-wagon)

"That's a bad way to legislate and a bad way to seek compliance," Saunders warns. "I don't think legislators are ill-intending. I just don't think they fully appreciate the burden associated with it."

## More to Come

New California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA) requirements will also lead to a big project for many companies. Many of the requirements are technically in effect, but mandatory cyber-risk audits and risk assessments will come into effect next year, says Saunders. CCPA will also add new, stricter requirements for sensitive information, data collection, and consent notices. The prep work starts now.

Finally, human resources AI laws and how they're being used in hiring, firing, and promotion decisions are another focus for companies going into 2026. Resume screening is one significant use case. With AI, HR teams can sort through 500 resumes in no time or use tools to parse out high performers.

But this raises discrimination and bias concerns — a significant risk related to all things AI. States are getting wise to these practices, and some have already passed laws that regulate the use of AI in the workforce, says Saunders. For example, [Illinois passed a law](https://www.ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=3773&GAID=17&DocTypeID=HB&SessionID=112&GA=103), amending its Human Rights Act to address rising discrimination concerns. It went into effect on Jan. 1.

"I think this year companies are catching up to the fact that these laws now exist," he says.

## Trump Administration 'Inconsistent' Regarding Cyber Policies

A [proposed amendment to the HIPAA Security Rule](/cyber-risk/industry-oppose-hipaa-security-rule-overhaul) is a big question for many clients, says Demian Ahn, data, cybersecurity, and privacy partner at Wilson Sonsini. He anticipates that the regulations may be less prescriptive than originally proposed, though others related to national security would fall in line with the DoJ's Data Security Program. One rule, the [Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure](/ics-ot-security/critical-infrastructure-ot-security-still-lags) (CIRCIA), is due to be [implemented in May](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/on-the-sixth-day-of-data-cisa-circia-6197765/).

However, predictions for the legal environment at the federal level in 2026 leave a lot of question marks.

"In 2025, the Trump administration has been inconsistent and a work in progress for cybersecurity," says Ahn. "There's a big difference between harmonization, which was a focus of many administration officials and members of congress, and just not doing regulations that were proposed."

If this trend continues, the administration will likely enforce existing laws and implement new ones for organizations that operate in industries with national security implications. In terms of cybersecurity posture, AI will continue to dominate the headlines.

## What Can Enterprises Expect at the State Level?

Going forward into the new year, companies can count on the continuation of state enforcement. Attorney general offices will likely view themselves as stepping into an era of less federal enforcement, with responsibility falling on the states, Ahn says. Essentially, they will step into a void that needs to be filled.

Saunders is on the same page and doesn't anticipate any significant legislation in the privacy or AI space on the federal level.

"If anything happens on the federal level, I'll give you a nickel," Saunders says. "I think it's going to continue to be on the state level, and frankly that's more complicated and introduces more burdensome compliance rubrics for companies."

Companies would prefer federal legislation, particularly in the privacy space, he adds. Having to ensure they're compliant with each state's varied legislation proves challenging. Additionally, it's difficult for lawmakers who don't understand AI or privacy as it relates to cybersecurity, to legislate it well, he says.

## Expect the Unexpected in 2026

Regardless of what is announced or enacted in 2026, figuring out which laws apply is one of the most challenging aspects for companies. It's challenging for lawyers, too, says Saunders, citing how each state likes to have its own definition that's worded only slightly differently.

"The fun thing about privacy in my world is there's going to be something this year that I didn't expect," Saunders says.

The idea that a company knows every single law in every jurisdiction is not an achievable goal, Saunders says, adding that there's no such thing as a 100% privacy-compliant company on the face of the planet. The advice for now is that companies do their best to stay on top of new laws, legislation, and compliance standards.

"The question is, 'How do you find the ones who are generating the most risk and will require the most investment?'" he says. "Stay on top of the big things, handle compliance with those, and there's usually an excellent trickle-down effect where you'll almost by accident comply with other laws that apply to you that you may not even know."

There's a big difference between harmonization, which was a focus of many administration officials and members of congress, and just not doing regulations that were proposed." - Demian Ahn, "If anything happens on the federal level, I'll give you a nickel. I think it's going to continue to be on the state level, and frankly that's more complicated and introduces more burdensome compliance rubrics for companies." - David Saunders, "The question is, 'How do you find the ones who are generating the most risk and will require the most investment?' Stay on top of the big things, handle compliance with those, and there's usually an excellent trickle-down effect where you'll almost by accident comply with other laws that apply to you that you may not even know." - David Saunders

This Dark Reading article (published January 12, 2026, by Arielle Waldman) examines the challenges enterprises face navigating privacy and cybersecurity laws in 2026. Key developments include:

**2025 Regulatory Actions:** The DoJ announced a new Data Security Program, the FTC updated COPPA rules, and HHS proposed amendments to the HIPAA Security Rule.

**Key Legal Priorities for 2026:**
1. **App Age Signal Laws:** State regulations requiring app stores and developers to verify ages during downloads. A Texas law (App Store Accountability Act) was temporarily blocked by a federal judge in late December; a Louisiana law was struck down; Utah enacted one in mid-2025. Companies struggle with assigning age ratings to every SKU.
2. **CCPA New Requirements:** Mandatory cyber-risk audits and risk assessments take effect, with stricter requirements for sensitive information, data collection, and consent notices.
3. **HR AI Regulations:** Laws regulating AI use in hiring, firing, and promotion decisions. Illinois passed a law amending its Human Rights Act effective Jan. 1, 2026, addressing discrimination concerns with AI resume screening.

**Federal-Level Uncertainty:** The Trump administration is described as "inconsistent" on cybersecurity policies. Experts anticipate limited federal privacy or AI legislation, with enforcement falling to state attorneys general. The CIRCIA rule is due for implementation in May 2026.

**Expert Quotes:** David Saunders (McDermott, Will, and Schulte) notes compliance is "made more challenging by the frequency of how quickly things change," and that expecting companies to comply with constantly changing rules "has a deterrent effect on compliance." Demian Ahn (Wilson Sonsini) states the Trump administration has been "inconsistent and a work in progress for cybersecurity."

The article concludes that achieving 100% privacy compliance is "not an achievable goal," and advises companies to focus on the highest-risk areas.

# SEC Proposes Rescission of Climate-Related Disclosure Rules

For Immediate Release

Washington D.C., May 29, 2026 —

The Securities and Exchange Commission today proposed the rescission of overly burdensome and costly rules that require companies to provide certain climate-related information in their registration statements and annual reports. The Commission’s proposal focuses on returning the agency to its core mandate – in line with its legal authority – and restoring a materiality-focused approach to securities regulation.

“SEC disclosure obligations should comply with the Commission’s statutory authority, be guided by materiality as the North Star, avoid the practical effect of dictating corporate behavior, and be imposed only when the expected benefits justify the likely costs and burdens,” said SEC Chairman Paul S. Atkins in a [statement](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/atkins-statement-rescission-climate-related-disclosure-rules-052926).

The Commission in March 2024 [approved amendments to its rules](https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/2024/03/s7-10-22) under the Securities Act of 1933 and Securities Exchange Act of 1934 to mandate highly specific and granular disclosure from virtually all public companies about climate-related matters such as greenhouse gas emissions, management of climate-related risks, and the financial statement effects of severe weather events.

On April 4, 2024, the Commission stayed the climate disclosure rules pending completion of consolidated litigation in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit. On March 27, 2025, the Commission [voted to end its defense](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2025-58) of the final rules. On Sept. 12, 2025, the Eighth Circuit issued an order holding the consolidated petitions for review in abeyance until such time as the Commission reconsiders the challenged rules by notice-and-comment rulemaking or renews its defense of the climate disclosure rules.

The Commission is now proposing to rescind the climate disclosure rules in their entirety because they exceed the scope of the agency's statutory authority. Even if it had authority to adopt such final rules, the Commission believes there are independent, compelling policy reasons to rescind them entirely:

The public comment period will remain open for 60 days following the publication of the proposing release in the Federal Register.

On February 21, 2024, UHG’s Optum posted a systems update notifying the public that its subsidiary, Change, was “experiencing a network interruption related to a cyber security issue.”1 The following day, UHG filed Form 8-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), stating that the company had “identified a suspected nation-state associated cyber security threat actor had gained access to some of the Change information technology systems.”2 The filing further stated that UHG “proactively isolated the impacted systems from other connecting systems” in an attempt to protect patient and provider data and contain the threat.3 UHG further claimed that “the Company believes the network interruption is specific to Change systems,” an assertion we now know to be false. args.summary:
This document is a letter dated May 14, 2024, from Senator Bill Cassidy (Ranking Member of the Senate HELP Committee) to Andrew Witty, CEO of UnitedHealth Group (UHG), requesting detailed information about the February 21, 2024 cyberattack on Change Healthcare, a UHG subsidiary. Key details include:

- Change Healthcare is one of the largest medical claims clearinghouses in the U.S., processing ~15 billion healthcare transactions annually.
- On February 21, 2024, Change experienced a network interruption due to a cybersecurity issue. UHG later identified ALPHV Blackcat, a Russia-based ransomware group, as the perpetrator.
- The hackers allegedly stole at least six terabytes of data, including PHI/PII covering "a substantial proportion of people in America" — including military personnel, veterans, and patients. Data includes SSNs, medical/dental records, financial payment info, and insurance claims.
- UHG reportedly paid a $22 million ransom on March 1, 2024, but a second group (RansomHub) later claimed to have four terabytes of stolen data and threatened to sell it.
- On April 15, 2024, RansomHub published files containing patient personal information, billing files, insurance records, and medical information on the dark web.
- The attack caused massive disruptions: pharmacies (CVS, Walgreens, TRICARE) faced challenges dispensing medications; electronic prescribing, claim submission, and payment processing were halted; providers went weeks without pay.
- UHG advanced over $7 billion in funding to providers, but this did not fully address the financial hardship.
- The breach reportedly occurred because ALPHV Blackcat accessed UHG systems via a Citrix remote portal using Change legacy software that did not have multifactor authentication (MFA) enabled.
- The December 2023 FBI/CISA/HHS joint advisory had warned about ALPHV Blackcat targeting healthcare and recommended MFA — which UHG had not implemented on the compromised system.
- Court filings from December 2021 (challenging the Change/Optum merger) revealed UHG's internal audit rated its data management as "Needs Improvement," citing "heightened risk of data being mismanaged" and "no effective means of enforcement" for data misuse.

The letter poses 20 detailed questions across three categories: (1) UHG's data governance framework generally, (2) data governance prior to the cyberattack, and (3) data governance after the attack — requesting responses by May 28, 2024.

# Change Healthcare Cyberattack Underscores Urgent Need to Strengthen Cyber Preparedness for Individual Health Care Organizations and as a Field

**The cyberattack on Change Healthcare in February 2024 disrupted health care operations on an unprecedented national scale, endangering patients' access to care, disrupting critical clinical and eligibility operations, and threatening the solvency of the nation's provider network. It demonstrated that the national consequences of cyberattacks targeting mission-critical third-party providers can be even more devastating than when hospitals or health systems are attacked directly.**

## Incident Overview

### Attack Target

Change Healthcare, a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group, is the predominant source of more than 100 critical functions that keep the U.S. health care system operating. It annually processes 15 billion health care transactions — touching 1 in every 3 patient records — including insurance eligibility verification and authorization, drug prescriptions, claims transmittals and payment.

### What Happened

On Feb. 21, 2024, an attack by the Russian ransomware group ALPHV BlackCat encrypted and incapacitated significant portions of Change Healthcare’s functionality.

### Impact

The attack had significant care delivery and financial consequences for patients, providers and communities, endangering patients and threatening the solvency of U.S. health care providers. Every hospital in the country felt the impact, either directly or indirectly. Impacts varied depending on factors such as amount of cash reserves, vendor redundancy and reliance on Change Healthcare technology.

A March 2024 AHA survey of nearly 1,000 hospitals found:

* 74% reported direct patient care impact, including delays in authorizations for medically necessary care.
* 94% reported the attack impacted them financially.
* 33% reported the attack disrupted more than half of their revenue.
* 60% reported requiring two weeks to three months to resume normal operations once Change Healthcare’s full functionality was re-established.

Many providers were forced to seek alternate ways — including pulling from reserves or taking out private loans — to pay clinician and care team salaries, acquire necessary medicine and supplies, and pay for critical physical security, dietary and environmental services contract work. The need to rely on less efficient manual processes in place of electronic ones also added substantial administrative costs.

### AHA Response

The AHA mobilized swiftly and served as a leading voice in the entire health care sector during the crisis. To facilitate collaboration, provide input and secure support, the AHA immediately engaged with top contacts at the White House, Congress, FBI, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA).

As UnitedHealth Group downplayed the severity of the event over the ensuing weeks, the AHA, among other actions, consistently set the record straight, informed the media and testified before Congress. These efforts ensured that Change Healthcare, not hospitals, bore responsibility for notifying patients of any data breach.

According to Kodiak Solutions, a revenue cycle data analytics firm, **the attack caused the value of claims submitted to drop $6.3 billion for their 1,850 hospital and 250,000 physician clients alone in just the first three weeks after the attack.**

# UnitedHealthcare Data Breach: A Guide to UnitedHealth Group's Major Incidents

One corporate giant, two ransomware attacks, and nearly 200 million Americans' health data exposed.

All of our content is written by humans, not robots. [Learn More](/editorial-guidelines/#written-by-humans)

[Gene Petrino](https://www.security.org/author/gene-petrino/)  ,  Security Advisor; Retired SWAT Commander

Last Updated Jul 8, 2026

By  [Gene Petrino](https://www.security.org/author/gene-petrino/)   Jul 8, 2026

the  **security**.brief

---

A 2024 cyberattack on UnitedHealthcare exposed sensitive data from millions of patients, including health and insurance information.

Navigate to:

* [Understanding UnitedHealth Group and Its Subsidiaries](#understanding)
* [Breach One: Change Healthcare (February 2024)](#one)
* [Breach Two: Episource (February 2025)](#two)
* [Both Incidents at a Glance](#both)
* [What Affected Members Should Do](#what)
* [When Your Healthcare Provider Becomes a Data Liability](#when)

It’s one of the largest and most disruptive healthcare [data breaches](https://www.security.org/identity-theft/breach/) in American history. The UnitedHealthcare data breach involves not just one company but a sprawling corporate family under UnitedHealth Group, the largest health insurer in the United States. Two of its subsidiaries suffered major cyberattacks within roughly a year of each other, and the combined reach of those incidents extends to nearly 200 million Americans.

Understanding which company was breached, what was taken, and what it means for you requires a brief orientation to how UnitedHealth Group is structured. This guide covers both the 2024 Change Healthcare ransomware attack and the 2025 Episource breach, explains what data was involved in each, and walks through what affected individuals should do to avoid [identity theft](https://www.security.org/identity-theft/).

**>> Find Out:** [How to Protect Yourself From Identity Theft](https://www.security.org/identity-theft/protection/)

## Understanding UnitedHealth Group and Its Subsidiaries

UnitedHealth Group (UHG) is a publicly traded corporation that operates two major business divisions. One is UnitedHealthcare, which is the health insurance arm and one of the largest insurers in the country. The other is Optum, which delivers healthcare services ranging from pharmacy benefits and direct care to the IT infrastructure that underlies much of the U.S. healthcare system.

Both Change Healthcare and Episource are subsidiaries of Optum. That means they sit under the UnitedHealth Group corporate umbrella but operate separately from UnitedHealthcare, the insurance brand that most members interact with directly. A cyberattack on Change Healthcare or Episource is technically an attack on an Optum subsidiary, not on the insurance company itself. But because those subsidiaries handle data that flows from and to UnitedHealthcare members and their providers, the downstream impact on UnitedHealthcare members has been significant.

## Breach One: Change Healthcare (February 2024)

On February 12, 2024, attackers affiliated with the ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware group gained access to Change Healthcare’s systems through a Citrix remote access portal that lacked multi-factor authentication. Change Healthcare is the largest healthcare payment clearinghouse in the United States, processing approximately 15 billion transactions per year and touching one in every three patient records.1

The attackers spent nine days moving through the network before deploying ransomware on February 21, 2024, the day the [Change Healthcare data breach](https://www.security.org/identity-theft/breach/change-healthcare/) was detected. That’s also when Change Healthcare started shutting down systems. During that window – February 17 and February 20 – the attackers exfiltrated an estimated 4 to 6 terabytes of data before the encryption began.

UnitedHealth Group’s CEO confirmed that the entry point lacked [multi-factor authentication](https://www.security.org/digital-safety/authentication-guide-how-to/) and that Change Healthcare had not updated its internal security procedures following UHG’s acquisition of the company in October 2022. Senator Ron Wyden summarized the failure: “This hack could have been stopped with cybersecurity 101.”2

### The Ransom and the Double Extortion

On March 1, 2024, UHG paid a $22 million ransom in Bitcoin through its Optum subsidiary in exchange for a promise that the stolen data would be deleted. The payment did not resolve the situation. ALPHV/BlackCat’s leadership conducted an exit scam. They took the ransom money and shut down their operation without paying the affiliate who had actually carried out the attack. That affiliate retained a copy of the stolen data and then partnered with RansomHub to launch a separate extortion campaign against Change Healthcare in April 2024. Patient data began appearing on [dark web](https://www.security.org/identity-theft/dark-web/) leak sites despite the $22 million payment.

**>> Check Out:** [The Best Identity Theft Protection with Dark Web Monitoring](https://www.security.org/identity-theft/best/dark-web-monitoring/)

### Who Was Affected and What Was Stolen

Change Healthcare’s final confirmed count stands at 192.7 million people, the largest healthcare data breach ever reported to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. That figure represents approximately 57% of the U.S. population in 2024. Individual notifications began going out in late July 2024 and continued on a rolling basis through 2025.

The categories of data exposed varied by individual but included:

| Category | Data Involved |
| --- | --- |
| Health information | Medical record numbers, providers, diagnoses, medications, test results, images, care and treatment details |
| Insurance information | Health plan and policy details, insurance company names, member/group ID numbers, Medicare/Medicaid IDs |
| Billing and claims | Claim numbers, account numbers, billing codes, balance information |
| Personal identifiers | Names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, email addresses; Social Security numbers and ID numbers in some cases |
| Financial information | Payment card numbers and banking information in limited cases |

Change Healthcare noted that for the majority of people affected, Social Security numbers were not part of the exposed data. However, the combination of diagnoses, treatment records, insurance details, and personal identifiers still constitutes an unusually comprehensive picture of a person’s medical life. The total financial cost to UnitedHealth Group reached approximately $3.1 billion in direct breach response costs through 2024.3

## Breach Two: Episource (February 2025)

### What Happened

Less than a year after the Change Healthcare attack, another UHG subsidiary suffered a major breach. Episource, a medical coding and risk adjustment company acquired by UHG’s Optum subsidiary in 2023, detected unusual activity on its computer network on February 6, 2025. A forensic investigation confirmed that attackers had been inside the system for approximately 10 days, between January 27 and February 6, 2025. One of Episource’s affected clients, Sharp Healthcare, confirmed the incident was caused by ransomware.

Episource shut down its systems upon detection, notified law enforcement, and engaged third-party cybersecurity experts. Individual notification letters began going out on a rolling basis from April 23, 2025. The breach was reported to the California Attorney General in June 2025.

### Who Was Affected and What Was Stolen

The HHS Office for Civil Rights breach portal lists 5,418,866 individuals as affected by the Episource breach, making it one of the largest healthcare data breaches of 2025. The stolen data varied by individual but could include names, postal and email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, Social Security numbers in some cases, health insurance policy details, Medicare and Medicaid identification numbers, and protected health information, including diagnoses, medications, test results, imaging, and medical record numbers.

Episource had not publicly identified the specific threat actor responsible, and at the time of reporting, had found no evidence of the stolen data being misused. The company offered two years of free credit monitoring and [identity theft protection services](https://www.security.org/identity-theft/best/) to affected individuals.

How to Get Your Exposed Data Offline
